questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to get better at learning German and I had heard that their Anthropology department was quite good. It is also NOT necessary to be fluent in German and there are plenty of classes English. I also enjoy classical music, which there is plenty of good and cheap opportunity to listen to in Vienna.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: While the city and the department and everything was great, I do feel that the classes in Denmark are better structured.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: After arriving it was great! The Department is not very big, so it was very easy to contact everyone and get help for stuff.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I recieved assistance in how to get the residence registration and the EU-residence, also help for registering for classes (class registration is usually only a couple weeks before the classes start).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was really not bad! If you want to stay at a dorm you have to apply immediately, like already in November/December if possible. I started applying in May and that was way too late. Then I went on WG-gesucht, which is an amazing website and super secure! I wrote to about 40-50 people, got 3 interviews and offered 2 places. WG-gesucht is definitely the place to go to find a place, especially since Facebook isn't a thing used in Austria.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It isn't possible to live "on" campus, it's basically like here in Copenhagen, it's very common to rent a room in an apartment. It's usual to pay between €500-800, personally I paid €610 for 14m2 and access to kitchen, two bathrooms, living room, and a balcony.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was pretty straightforward, but the department is always happy to help if something isn't working! Also pretty much guaranteed to get the courses you want, as exchange students are prioritised in the selection.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You can find all the courses on u:find where you can also sort by language. Personally I didn't really find the website very user friendly, but it gets the job done. Often they don't put the courses until a month before the classes start, so it's hard to plan ahead. You can however register for more classes than you need, try them out, and then deregister within a week or two. Something to be aware of though: they have mandatory attendance for seminars (SE), but not for lectures (VO). So while seminars might be easier to make friends, you would have to show up for almost every single one, and have to do make-up work for classes that you miss.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The department was very kind to help if anything was unclear. The teachers are generally very helpful and are willing to answer all questions over e-mail! Even before you arrive at the uni.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted, they prioritise exchange students in registration.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember to check whether it's a seminar (SE) or a lecture (VO), since I almost only signed up for seminars and had to show up for all classes. Seminars also have continuous assesment, meaning there's mandatory participation and often smaller assignments throughout the semester - I often had to hand in my notes for each text every week, to prove I had done the reading. Lectures usually only have a final exam with no assignments throughout.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My experience was that Copenhagen generally has a better program, but there are some great teachers at Vienna as well. I also had some interesting courses, and the good thing about Vienna is that you're allowed to take both Bachelor's and Master's courses so there's a big pool to choose from! You can also take classes from other institutes, but you need the approval from the head of those institutes - definitely ask the department of anthropology for help with this, as I am sure they will help!

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses are smaller than at CPH (usually 5 ECTS), so you need to have many more courses than usual. Of course since they are pretty small courses, they are not as difficult either.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I really liked many of the teachers! However the seminars are way more focused on student participation, which sometimes was great and sometimes not so great.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:

240029-1 SE BM5 Ethnographic reading: Making Kin in the Anthropocene: Reading Donna Haraway and Anna Tsing

240038-1 SE BM7 Observing Society - Anthropologies of Social Reproduction

240044-1 PR BM8 Ethnographisches Feldpraktikum

240017-1 VO BM3 Theoretical Traditions and Developments in Anthropology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Anything with Andreas Streinzer, amazing teacher. Also the Empire and Capital class was great, but I'm pretty sure the teacher has gotten a job in Scotland now.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing - a lot of stuff is cheaper than in Denmark, however the museums are quite expensive, usually around €20. It might be a good idea to get either the KHM or the Bundesmuseen Jahreskarte (årskort).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Museums more expensive, coffee and beer less expensive. They do also give 5-10% tip, which I had to get used to.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Go to the sports institute for classes, kinda like the KU idræt! Many many things, but be aware of the deadline as everything is booked quickly. They ahve pole dancing, pilates, football, crossfit, martial arts, etcetc

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The uni itself has really limited social options unfortunately, but the rest of the city is filled with stuff to do. All the exchange students created a massive whatsapp group where everyone would invite people to do stuff.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Museums, concerts, (wine-)hiking, sports, churches, cafés, bars.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Museums, concerts, (wine-)hiking, sports, churches, cafés, bars.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, it's not so different from DK culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I didn't actually make friends with any local students, only the austrians I lived with. It's hard since they know that you're leaving, so they don't want to be close.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Café culture! I love going to cafés and bars, which is very cheap here.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: You DON'T have to be able to speak german, having had german in gymnasiet (high school) is enough! There are many English courses and you will never need to use German. Also always ask the department for help with anything, they will be more than happy to help with whatever.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Only that you DON'T NEED TO SPEAK GERMAN.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know other people, learning that there's a whole world of different people and different ways of being and experiencing the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: You constantly meet new people, which is great, but it's also hard to get real deep friendships in such a short amount of time. I kinda regret not staying for a whole year, since that's pretty common for other countries.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
